chapters.title: Chapter 5: Matching the Method to the Business

lessons.title: Valuing Cyclicals: Metals, Cement and Autos

children.text: A steel company trading at 4 times earnings with record profits sounds like the bargain of the decade. It is usually the opposite. For cyclical businesses the P/E ratio runs backwards: it is at its lowest when the stock is most dangerous, and at its highest, or meaningless, when the opportunity is best. Metals, cement, autos, sugar, paper, chemicals and shipping all behave this way, and together they make up a large part of the Indian listed market.

body.text: For a cyclical, the number you need is not next year's profit but mid-cycle profit. Value the whole cycle, not the moment you happen to be looking at.

children.text: A cyclical company's earnings swing far more than the value of its business. A steel plant earning ₹18,000 of

in a boom and ₹4,000 in a downturn is the same plant, with the same furnaces, mines and customers. The market knows this, so the share price moves much less than earnings. The P/E therefore collapses at the top of the cycle and explodes, or turns negative, at the bottom.

markDefs.definition: Operating profit before depreciation divided by tonnes sold. The standard profitability measure for commodity producers such as steel and cement, because it shows the spread between realisations and costs, independent of volume.

children.text: Vidarbha Steel Ltd is a fictional NSE-listed producer with 5 million tonnes of capacity running at 85.0% utilisation, so it sells about 4.3 million tonnes a year. Depreciation is ₹1,200 crore, interest ₹700 crore, net debt ₹8,000 crore, book value ₹12,000 crore, and it has 45 crore shares. Suppose the market values it at ₹361 per share throughout the cycle, roughly 6 times mid-cycle EBITDA.

body.text: The P/E of 3.8× in the peak year is not a valuation signal, it is a warning. Peak profits attract new capacity from every producer in the industry, which eventually drives spreads back down. The stocks that screen cheapest on trailing P/E during a commodity boom are often the ones with the most to lose.

children.text: are the foundation of every cyclical valuation. There are four practical ways to estimate them for Indian companies.

markDefs.definition: An estimate of what a company would earn in a typical, mid-cycle year rather than in an unusually strong or weak one. The basis for valuing cyclical businesses.

body.caption: Ways to normalise a cyclical's earnings

cells: Average EBITDA per tonne over a full cycle, multiplied by realistic volumes
Apply the 7 to 10 year average EBITDA margin to current or normalised revenue
Apply a mid-cycle ROE to current book value to estimate normal profit
Any cyclical with a stable asset base; pairs naturally with P/B
Model the gap between output prices and key input costs at long-run levels
Steel (realisation minus iron ore and coking coal), refining, sugar

children.text: For Vidarbha Steel, mid-cycle EBITDA per tonne of ₹9,500 on 4.3 million tonnes gives EBITDA of ₹4,038 crore. At 6 times, that is an enterprise value of ₹24,225 crore. Subtract ₹8,000 crore of net debt and divide by 45 crore shares: ₹361 per share. Cross-check against the balance sheet: that is 1.4 times book value for a business whose mid-cycle ROE is about 13.4%, against 35.9% in the peak year.

body.label: The cyclical valuation rule
body.context: Never apply a peak multiple to peak earnings, or a trough multiple to trough earnings. Both double-count the cycle and produce extreme answers.

children.text: Commodity businesses have a second anchor that most other companies lack: what it would cost to build the same capacity today. If enterprise value per tonne is far below replacement cost, no rational competitor will build new capacity, which eventually tightens supply and lifts prices. If it is far above, new capacity is coming.

stats.label: Illustrative replacement cost
stats.context: Cost of building new integrated steel capacity

stats.label: Kaveri Ridge Cement: EV per tonne
Illustrative cement replacement cost
stats.context: Greenfield cost of new cement capacity

children.text: Kaveri Ridge, the cement company from Chapters 2 and 3, carries an enterprise value of about ₹4,027 per tonne of post-expansion capacity, well below the illustrative ₹7,000 per tonne cost of building new capacity. That is a supportive signal: buying capacity through the stock market is cheaper than building it. Indian cement deals are often discussed in exactly these terms, and acquirers watch the gap closely.

body.text: Replacement cost is a floor argument, not a valuation. A plant in a poor location, with old technology or no limestone reserves, can trade below replacement cost forever and deserve to. Use the comparison to judge whether new supply is likely, then value the business on mid-cycle cash flows.

Sector on every brokerage buy list

body.title: How external shocks move an Indian steel cycle

events.title: Import pressure
events.description: A surge of cheap imported steel pushed domestic prices down and squeezed Indian producers. The government responded with trade measures, including a minimum import price.

events.title: Pandemic collapse and recovery
events.description: Demand and prices fell sharply during lockdowns, then recovered quickly as construction and manufacturing restarted.

events.title: Record spreads
events.description: Global supply disruption lifted steel prices to unusually high levels, producing record profits and very low trailing P/E ratios.

events.title: Export duty
events.description: The government imposed an export duty on several steel products to cool domestic prices. Export volumes and margins fell.

events.title: Duty withdrawn
events.description: The export duty was rolled back and the cycle moved on. None of these shocks changed the long-run value of a tonne of capacity as much as they changed a single year's earnings.

children.text: Autos: A Different Kind of Cycle
Auto companies are cyclical too, but their cycle has three layers stacked on top of each other, and a valuation that ignores any one of them will be wrong.

body.title: The three layers of an auto cycle

columns.label: What moves volumes
points: Economic cycle: incomes, interest rates, availability of financing
Rural demand and monsoons, especially for two-wheelers and tractors
Replacement cycles, typically several years long
Regulation: emission and safety norms that raise vehicle prices

columns.label: What moves margins and value
points: Product cycle: a successful new model can lift share and margins for years
Raw material costs: steel, aluminium, precious metals, semiconductors
Operating leverage: high fixed costs magnify volume swings
The shift to electric vehicles, which changes capital needs and competition

body.caption: Valuing an Indian auto company, piece by piece

cells: EV/EBITDA on mid-cycle volumes and margins, or a DCF across a full cycle
Value separately on P/B and ROE, never inside an EV/EBITDA multiple
Value separately, at market value where listed
Model as a scenario: capital spending now, uncertain returns later

body.text: Never apply a single EV/EBITDA multiple to a consolidated auto group that includes a large lending subsidiary. For a lender, borrowings are raw material rather than financing, so consolidated net debt becomes meaningless. The lessons on lenders and on sum-of-the-parts later in this chapter deal with both problems.

body.title: Mid-cycle EBITDA
body.prompt: An aluminium producer sells 3 million tonnes a year. Its EBITDA per tonne over the last full cycle has averaged ₹8,000. What is its mid-cycle EBITDA, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: 3 million tonnes × ₹8,000 per tonne = ₹2,400 crore. In crore terms: 3 × 8,000 ÷ 10 = ₹2,400 crore. Apply a mid-cycle EV/EBITDA multiple to this figure, not to the current year's.

body.title: Enterprise value per tonne
body.prompt: A cement company has an enterprise value of ₹12,000 crore and capacity of 8 million tonnes. What is its EV per tonne of capacity, in ₹?
body.explanation: ₹12,000 crore ÷ 8 million tonnes = ₹15,000 per tonne. Compare that with the cost of building new capacity to judge whether fresh supply is likely.

body.title: The 4× steel stock
body.question: A steel company reports record annual profit and trades at 4 times trailing earnings, against a market average of 22 times. Steel prices are at a multi-year high and every major producer has announced expansions. What is the most sensible interpretation?
options: The stock is deeply undervalued and should rerate towards the market multiple
Earnings are near a cyclical peak, so the low P/E reflects profits unlikely to repeat; value it on mid-cycle earnings instead
The P/E is low because the company is poorly managed
Trailing P/E is the right measure here because it uses reported, audited numbers
body.explanation: A very low P/E at the top of a commodity cycle usually signals that the market expects earnings to fall, not that the stock is mispriced. Industry-wide expansion announcements make a decline in spreads more likely. Normalise earnings before drawing any conclusion.

body.title: The right earnings
body.textWithBlank: Cyclical companies should be valued on ___ earnings, rather than on the profits of the most recent year.
body.explanation: Normalised, or mid-cycle, earnings represent what a company earns in a typical year, avoiding both peak and trough distortions.

body.title: The sugar stock at 3 times earnings
body.scenario: Manish, an investor in Kolhapur, is looking at a listed sugar company. It trades at 3.2 times trailing earnings and 1.9 times book value after a year of exceptionally high sugar realisations and strong ethanol demand. Its EBITDA margin last year was 24%, against a ten-year average of 11%. It has announced a debt-funded expansion of its crushing capacity, as have three other listed sugar companies. A friend tells him: "Three times earnings, you cannot lose."
body.prompt: How should Manish value this company, and what should worry him?
body.modelAnswer:
1. The P/E is low because earnings are high, not because the stock is cheap. A 24% margin against a ten-year average of 11% means last year was close to a peak.
2. Normalise first. Apply the ten-year average margin, or a mid-cycle EBITDA per tonne of cane crushed, to realistic volumes. At an 11% margin, earnings would be far lower and the P/E far higher than 3.2 times.
3. The P/B of 1.9 times is the more revealing number. For a cyclical near a peak, P/B judged against normalised ROE is usually a better guide than P/E. He should ask what ROE this company earns in an average year.
4. Industry-wide debt-funded expansion is a classic late-cycle signal. New crushing capacity across four listed companies will arrive just as prices normalise.
5. Sugar carries policy risk in both directions. Cane pricing, export restrictions and ethanol blending policy can change margins quickly.

What to do: value the company on mid-cycle margins with a mid-cycle EV/EBITDA multiple; check net debt after the announced expansion, since leverage is what turns a downturn into distress; and only then compare the result with the market price. If it still looks cheap on normalised numbers, the opportunity is real.

points: For cyclicals, P/E runs backwards: lowest at the peak, highest or meaningless at the trough.
Value them on normalised, mid-cycle earnings using mid-cycle unit economics, average margins, normalised ROE or spread analysis.
Apply a mid-cycle multiple to mid-cycle earnings. Never combine peak with peak or trough with trough.
P/B judged against a normalised ROE is often a steadier guide than P/E for commodity producers.
Compare EV per tonne with replacement cost to judge whether new supply is coming, as a check rather than a valuation.
Autos stack an economic cycle, a product cycle and a technology shift; value captive finance arms separately from the manufacturing business.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Vidarbha Steel Ltd, Kaveri Ridge Cement Ltd, the other companies described and the individuals named are fictional, and all figures, including replacement costs and multiples, are illustrative. The steel timeline is a simplified summary of publicly reported events. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before making investment decisions.
